newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: WIK DECISION IN THE HIGH COURT TODAY
The High Court today will hand down another landmark decision on the native title issue.
The Wik People from Cape York Peninsula have asked the High Court to rule on whether pastoral leases extinguish native title - or whether the two can co-exist.
Governments, Aboriginal groups and the pastoral industry are looking to the High Court to clear up the issue.

If the High Court rules that native title and pastoral leases can co-exist, the pastoral industry and State and Territory governments may renew calls for the Federal Government to change the Native Title Act.
Today's decision may not finalise the issue and more cases may be required to clarify the issue in each State and Territory.
BOLKUS CONDEMNS TREATMENT OF BOYS IN HANSON SPITTING CASE
The Shadow Justice Minister says the detention in custody of two young Aborigines for allegedly spitting at MP Pauline Hanson could make Australia a further target for international criticism.
The boys, aged 11 and 12 are on remand for four weeks, after a magistrate refused to allow them bail over the incident at the Queensland M.P's office.
Nick Bolkus says the action goes against the Aboriginal deaths in custody recommendations.
He says Australia's international reputation regarding human rights could take a battering over the case.
VICTORIAN LABOR PARTY VOTES ON A SPILL MOTION
The Victorian Labor Party caucus will be voting today on a spill of all positions including the party's leader.
The meeting was called by leader John Brumby who has announced that all party jobs, including his own, are up for grabs.
The spill follows a factional deal between the right wing Labor Unity group and some members of the left designed to revitalise the party.
Mr Brumby is expected to be returned as leader.
SURVEY SHOWS MORE POSITIVE ECONOMIC OUTLOOK
There's positive news this morning on the economic front with the best trends in manufacturing for almost two years.
The December quarter survey shows the first positive trends in production, sales and orders in 21-months.
Investment has also increased after falling in each of the past eight quarters.
Allan Handberg, Chief Executive of the Australian Chamber of Manufactures describes the pick-up as modest.
He says there's a downside with the survey indicating profits continue to be disappointing, export growth remains weak and more job losses are expected.
INCENTIVES SOUGHT TO REDUCE THE AGE OF CARS
New South Wales' largest motoring organisation says the Federal Government should cut sales tax on new cars as an incentive to reduce the age of cars on Australia's roads.
The call follows a new CSIRO study which shows people in cars more than 11 years old, are almost twice as likely to die in road accidents as those in newer cars which have better safety features.
The NRMA's vehicles and environment manager, Jack Haley says that since 1971, the average age of cars has risen from five to ten years.
